title: Preface
summary: A declassified CORONA reconnaissance satellite history (released 2018, classified NOFORN-ORCON) by Frederic Oder, James Fitzpatrick, and Paul Worthman, dated November 1987. It includes a table of contents covering the Cold War closed-society problem, Open Skies, WS-117L origins, Sputnik, ARPA, Discoverer, contractor and camera selection, security, NRO and CIA roles, flight programs, imagery achievements, and appendices with representative imagery, references, and an index. It also lists illustrations of key officials and charts, and its preface describes earlier histories by Robert Perry and Helen Kleyla and the work's sponsorship.

title: Section 1
summary: Post-WWII US national security faced a closed Soviet society, requiring intelligence on USSR interior. Collection options were limited (signals sites, difficult agent operations), prompting overhead reconnaissance: the U-2 program, and earlier RAND's 1946 satellite feasibility study (Project RAND), which in 1954 concluded satellite photography could majorly reverse US strategic intelligence posture. The report traces how reconnaissance need and new missile/rocket technology made space photographic reconnaissance the main source of critical imagery.

title: Section 2

nodes.title: Section 2 (intro)
nodes.summary: Declassified history of Weapon System 117L (WS-117L), the Advanced Reconnaissance System. Covers the U-2's limited lifespan after 1956 Soviet radar tracking, the first successful air catch of satellite film capsule in August 1960, and WS-117L origins: RAND studies, the Atlas ICBM link, WDD management, the 1956 development plan and funding shortfalls, the three-phase test plan with E/F payload designations, design bidders, and budget and 'space for peace' policy obstacles.

nodes.title: Open Skies
Open Skies (intro)
nodes.summary: Covers Cold War space and overflight policy: uncertainty over the legality of satellite operations under international law, with little official attention. In 1955 Eisenhower proposed 'mutual air reconnaissance' (Open Skies); the USSR endorsed it in principle but opposed it, and announced its own scientific satellites with photographic equipment. Overflight was a customary intelligence tool, illustrated by the 1956 GENETRIX balloon program. Leghorn argued for covert satellite reconnaissance under WS-117L, which faced budget cuts in 1956.

nodes.title: An Alternative: 'Second Story'
nodes.summary: Describes 'Second Story,' an alternative approach to the WS-117L reconnaissance satellite program, proposed by Colonel Oder to General Schriever in 1957 when funds were expected to be nonexistent. It combined covert overflight, CIA participation, and acceleration, pairing an announced WS-117L cancellation with an overt Air Force scientific satellite and covert reconnaissance under CIA oversight. Attempts to gain funding failed, ARDC's endorsement was unhelpful, and the Stewart Committee was revived. After Sputnik, McElroy approved acceleration, though reluctance to sponsor an open reconnaissance satellite persisted. Program challenges included funding, schedule slippage, security, and engineering demands. Finally, the President's Board of Consultants reported on advanced reconnaissance options, and a joint status report was requested.

Cold War overflight and space policy: legality of satellite operations was uncertain. Eisenhower's 1955 Open Skies proposal was endorsed in principle but opposed by the USSR, which launched photographic scientific satellites; overflight was a customary intelligence tool (GENETRIX balloons, 1956). Leghorn pushed covert reconnaissance under WS-117L, which faced cuts. 'Second Story' (Oder, 1957) combined covert overflight, CIA role, and acceleration with an overt Air Force satellite; funding failed, the Stewart Committee was revived, and after Sputnik McElroy approved acceleration. Challenges included funding, schedule, security, and engineering; the Board of Consultants reviewed options and a joint status report was requested.

nodes.title: CORONA is Born
nodes.summary: Declassified history of CIA-Air Force Project CORONA, the first US reconnaissance satellite program. After Sputnik, WS-117L's most promising part was split off under joint CIA-Air Force management, modeled on the U-2 effort. Proposals for Thor-boosted interim systems came from Horner, RAND (including recovery techniques), Teller's group, and General Electric. Lockheed and BMD pursued a Thor-Hustler (Agena) approach. Early 1958 discussions led to Eisenhower's approval, with CIA control and ARPA cover. ARPA's February 28, 1958 directive cancelled the Thor-boosted interim system and enabled covert reactivation, with personnel and contractor reactions noted.

nodes.title: Discoverer and CORONA
nodes.summary: Describes how CORONA, after removal from WS-117L and moved to covert management, was disguised as the Air Force scientific program Discoverer, which justified overt procurement of boosters, stages, biomedical cover launches, and launch facilities while only the reconnaissance components stayed covert. After Bissell and Ritland arranged the overt cancellation and covert reactivation, the design used a Thor first stage and an Agena second stage. On 28 February 1958, Schriever and Oder met CIA and Lockheed representatives as the signed ARPA directive reached BMD, arranged informing General Electric and Fairchild, and reviewed camera and vehicle subsystem proposals.

nodes.title: CORONA Design Evolution and Contractor Selections
nodes.summary: The text covers the CORONA reconnaissance program's design evolution in 1958. Four contractor proposals initially favored spin-stabilized vehicles, with disputes over recovering only the nose cone versus the whole vehicle. Itek acquired Boston University's Physics Research Lab, strengthening its bid. CIA, BMD, and ARPA coordinated security, contract cancellations, and a covert 'black' environment. Film recovery was chosen, with General Electric as recovery vehicle contractor. A Cambridge panel picked Itek as backup camera contractor. At San Mateo meetings, schedules, launch site (Cooke AFB), and a 10-vehicle procurement were set. Bissell ultimately chose Itek's three-axis stabilized high-acuity camera over Fairchild's spin-stabilized design, and revised the project cost estimate from $20 to $31 million.

nodes.title: Formal CORONA Proposal to the President
nodes.summary: Formal CORONA proposal to the President for a short-lived reconnaissance satellite with a recoverable film capsule (20-foot resolution, 12 planned launches, operational ~June 1959, approved 16 April 1958, only 10 funded). Covers agency roles: ARPA technical supervision, Air Force BMD execution and ground support, CIA covert equipment procurement and security. Describes management: Bissell and Ritland leadership, looser joint authority than U-2, Bissell's direct control via meetings, and CIA liaison at Lockheed.

nodes.title: 1958 CORONA Organization Chart
nodes.summary: Describes the 1958 CORONA reconnaissance satellite program: a cooperative Air Force-CIA effort with roles for BMD, CIA (covert objectives, liaison with State), Lockheed (technical director, orbit stage, testing), GE (recovery capsule, camera), and Douglas (Thor boosters). Covers the schedule slip from a July 1958 target to a likely June 1959 first launch, the planned 12 vehicles as an interim program, and security arrangements including the covert 'Ranch' assembly facility at Hiller Helicopters, Menlo Park (1958-1969), cover stories, and briefing restrictions on personnel.

nodes.title: Problems of Growth and Change
nodes.summary: Describes CORONA's 1958-59 problems: cost overrun ($18M extra for Thor boosters, plus added vehicles, requiring presidential approval); Bissell's promotion to CIA Deputy Director for Plans and reorganization into the Development Project Division; management strain. Covers Air Force/DoD interference (Jupiter booster proposal blocked), Sheppard's role, cover stories, and the split of WS-117L into Discoverer (CORONA-Thor) and Sentry (Samos) series with biomedical animal payloads.

nodes.title: The CORONA launching Site
nodes.summary: Describes the CORONA satellite program's launch site and recovery planning. Vandenberg AFB was chosen for near-polar southward launches over the Pacific, with safety and Hawaii recovery advantages. Because launches could not be concealed, the air-sea recovery became an overt element, using the 6593d Test Squadron (Special) with C-119J aircraft, activated August 1958, plus tracking stations, a backup seaborne force, and a plan to move recovered capsules to secure channels.

nodes.title: CORONA Contractor Arrangements and Progress
nodes.summary: Describes CORONA program contractor issues: a 1960s-era dispute between Lockheed and General Electric over third-stage design and roles (prime vs. subcontractor), resolved in June with agreed work statements. Both firms followed CIA/Air Force-approved design philosophy favoring proven techniques, simplicity, and reliability. Milestones noted: design review in April/May, design freeze 26 July, drawings October. Technical progress appeared reasonable.

nodes.title: CORONA Management Arrangements: The ARPA factor Revisited
nodes.summary: The text covers management problems in the CORONA reconnaissance satellite program from September 1958 onward, caused by overlapping authority among ARPA, BMD, CIA, and the Administration. ARPA sought to redirect WS-117L funds and expand the program, prompting cost disputes: revised costs reached $129 million, Bissell protested, and Ritland and Sheppard explained the increases. Proposals to separate CORONA from Sentry, ARPA's new funding limits and 'user funds' policy, and Dr. Land's objections are discussed. The result was the creation of a separate 'Discoverer' program, with eight CORONA launches sponsored by ARPA and four funded by the Air Force.

nodes.title: Improving CORONA Cover and Security
nodes.summary: Describes how the CORONA reconnaissance program's cover and security were revised after Sentry was revealed as a reconnaissance satellite in late 1958. It covers needed cover stories (ARPA's role, polar orbit justification, recoverable capsules, camera explanations), planned leaks, and the decision to keep CORONA covert. It also details the 1959 funding crisis and the shift to a 25-flight noncovert Discoverer plan, which was then curbed through Horner's directive. It further covers letters between Lockheed and BMD meant to create a Secret cover explanation, and the 1959 ARGON geodetic satellite program placed under CORONA's security framework.

nodes.title: The Early Flight Program
The Early Flight Program (intro)
nodes.summary: Early CORONA/Discoverer satellite program (1959-1960): the 21 Jan 1959 launch aborted from premature rocket ignition; Discoverer-I reached orbit 28 Feb 1959 with no recovery capsule; Discoverer-II reached orbit but its capsule landed off target near Spitzbergen, Norway, and was never found, with a Soviet capture rumor. Discoverers III and IV failed to reach orbit due to Agena thrust shortfalls. Repeated failures angered President Eisenhower and strained Bissell's staff. Engineers found multiple weaknesses, and Lockheed was faulted for inadequate instrumentation. Discoverers VII-X also failed, and a sanitary-napkin cooling design was used on Discoverer IX.

nodes.title: Remarks
nodes.summary: Covers early CORONA (Discoverer) reconnaissance satellite flights of 1959-1960: a list of launch failures (capsule ejection, Agena orbit failures, retrorocket and camera malfunctions, bad orbits); AFBMD's persistence despite low reliability and expanded schedules for an Army mapping camera; Discoverer-XII's 1960 pad malfunction and Bissell's push to keep going; competing Samos program and political pressure; causes of failures (Thor burn timing, stabilization and recovery rocket faults); and the successful Discoverer-XIII/XIV recoveries, including Mathison's publicity-driven capsule handling and courier changes.

Covers the early CORONA/Discoverer reconnaissance satellite program (1959-1960). Launch failures included a premature-ignition abort, capsule ejection and retrorocket faults, Agena thrust and orbit failures, camera malfunctions, and a Discoverer-XII pad malfunction. Discoverer-II's capsule was never found. Eisenhower was angered, and Lockheed was faulted for instrumentation. AFBMD persisted despite low reliability, with the Samos program and political pressure in the background. Discoverer XIII and XIV achieved recoveries, including publicity-driven capsule handling.

summary: Declassified history of WS-117L and CORONA, the first US reconnaissance satellite program. Covers the U-2's limits after 1956, the 1960 air catch of a film capsule, and WS-117L origins (RAND, Atlas, funding, test phases). Covers Open Skies and 'Second Story', then Sputnik-driven acceleration. Details CORONA's CIA-Air Force split, Discoverer cover, contractor selections (Itek, GE, Lockheed), budget growth to $31M, management and ARPA disputes, Vandenberg launch and air recovery, cover and security, and early launch failures.

title: Section 3

nodes.title: Achievement: A New Vantage
Achievement: A New Vantage (intro)
nodes.summary: Describes Discoverer-XIV (August 1960), the first fully successful CORONA reconnaissance flight: its camera worked, the capsule was aerially recovered by Captain Mitchell's crew, and film yielded about 3,000 feet covering 1.65 million square miles at roughly 55 lines/mm resolution, identifying 35-foot objects. Eisenhower's secrecy wish led to the capsule being destroyed. Also covers the 1960 missile gap politics, the U-2 loss, Discoverer-XVIII's improvements (65 lines/mm, 25-foot objects), and key personnel, with Bissell credited most.

nodes.title: Corona Security: Assessment and Conjectures
nodes.summary: Covers CORONA satellite reconnaissance security from 1959-1962. Topics: why the Soviets may have accepted Discoverer as a non-military program (small size, cheap development style, capability, and publicized space efforts); the UN Committee on Peaceful Uses of Outer Space and Resolutions 1472 and 1721; US registration of launches, including the DoD's limits and Stevenson's concerns; CIA and DDR Scoville's opposition to renouncing reconnaissance; the BYEMAN security system and NRP; the Gilpatric Directive restricting launch information; NSAM 156 policy; and Killian and McCone's recommendations. The NSC approved secrecy in July 1962, which has continued.

nodes.title: The National Reconnaissance Office
nodes.summary: The text traces the origins of the National Reconnaissance Office (NRO). Rising satellite and overflight reconnaissance costs (near $300 million by 1961) prompted a formal DoD-CIA arrangement. Pressures included Air Force efforts to dominate space missions, unclear roles, and Bissell's shift away from CORONA toward covert action. Charyk's proposal led to the 6 September 1961 agreement creating the National Reconnaissance Program and NRO, with six elements covering scope, management, Air Force responsibilities, and tasking by the US Intelligence Board. The Air Force viewed the move as distrust by OSD, as Discoverer and Samos were removed from its command. Bissell's departure left Charyk as sole director, requiring further clarification.

Discoverer-XIV (August 1960) was the first fully successful CORONA flight: aerially recovered film covered 1.65 million square miles at about 55 lines/mm, identifying 35-foot objects; the capsule was later destroyed per Eisenhower's wish. Discoverer-XVIII improved to 65 lines/mm and 25-foot objects, with Bissell credited most. Covers Soviet acceptance of Discoverer as non-military, UN space resolutions, US launch registration, BYEMAN/NRP security, the Gilpatric Directive, NSAM 156, and the 1962 secrecy approval. Also traces the NRO's creation via the 6 September 1961 DoD-CIA agreement, amid Air Force-OSD tensions and Bissell's departure.

nodes.title: 1962 CORONA Organization Chart
nodes.summary: A 1962 CORONA organization chart and history of the NRO. Covers the second NRP Agreement establishing a single Director of the NRO (no deputy), Charyk's appointment and NRO directive organizing Programs A-D, and NRO staffing from Air Force, Navy, Army, CIA and NSA. Describes CORONA evolution: 1959 assumptions, the 1960 U-2 shootdown, the C-prime camera (KH-2) with better resolution, the stereo Mural (KH-4) system, competing Itek and Fairchild C-61 proposals, and rivalry with Samos, E-5, E-6 and GAMBIT programs.

nodes.title: a CORONA
a CORONA (intro)
a CORONA (intro)
nodes.summary: Describes CORONA reconnaissance satellite history: Eisenhower backed Land's 1960 plan to upgrade cameras (C'' camera with faster f/3.5 lens by Itek), costs rising from $3.5M to about $5M, improved resolution (20-25 ft vs 35 ft), and mission results: Discoverer launches with many failures in 1961, seven successful recoveries in 13 missions, and totals of 26 monoscopic missions with 12 successes.

nodes.title: Discoverer Flight Summary· 1960
nodes.summary: Declassified 1960 Discoverer flight summary table listing missions IX through XIX (mission numbers 9006-9013), with dates, camera type, and remarks. Most Agena rocket failures to orbit, spin rocket failure, a diagnostic flight, successful water pick-up, first successful airc atch, camera operating OK on several flights, wrong pitch on reentry, no recovery on some, a D-timer malfunction, payload malfunction, first successful C' flight, a radiometric payload, and one flight with no photo mission or recovery planned.

nodes.title: CORONA-Mural
nodes.summary: Describes the CORONA-Mural program: a 1960-61 proposal (initially named GEMINI by Lockheed) to combine two CORONA cameras into a stereo reconnaissance system for stereo coverage of denied areas. Covers Charyk's approval, the March 1961 halt by the Air Force, compartmentation and disclosure timing, the added Itek framing camera and Army Map Service concerns about mapping independence, the interim transitional role, and a table of CORONA/ARGON/Mural camera specifications, units launched, and recovery counts.

nodes.title: Camera Configurations and Characteristics
nodes.summary: Describes CORONA-M camera systems and Itek's 1962-63 M-2 (Mural-2) proposal, rejected by the Purcell panel in June 1963 but later reemerging as CORONA J-4. Covers the Samos E-5 failure and the LANYARD/KH-6 adaptation for Leningrad ABM sites, the February 1962 CORONA-M mission, production and launch schedules, and the E-6 payload's April 1962 launch with mixed results. Notes NRO follow-on orders and the six added CORONA-M systems, with resolution comparisons.

nodes.title: Discoverer Flight Summary - 1961
nodes.summary: Discoverer/CORONA reconnaissance mission history: a 1961 flight summary table (mission numbers, dates, camera types, outcomes such as Agena failures, water/air recoveries) and narrative on early ARGON and CORONA-M successes, E-6 Samos failures in 1962, the CORONA-J double-capsule design, and LANYARD/GAMBIT technology lineage under the NRO.

nodes.title: Discoverer Flight Summary - 1962
nodes.summary: A 1962 Discoverer flight summary lists CORONA/NRO missions (XXXVII-XXXVIII, 9030-9050) with dates, camera status, and outcomes. It describes Bissell's streamlined management, the 1962 split of the CIA Deputy Director for Plans into Plans and Research, and tensions over CORONA control among CIA, Air Force, and NRO leaders (McMillan, Scoville, Greer). It covers the Third and Funding Agreements of 1963, PFIAB criticism of McCone, Wheelon's appointment, the CORONA-J plan, early-1963 launch failures, and McCone's demand for reliable coverage. A Thor-booster diagram closes the text.

Describes the CORONA reconnaissance satellite program: its 1960 origins under Eisenhower and Land, rising costs and improved resolution, and mission results including Discoverer launch failures and recoveries. Covers the 1960 and 1961 flight summaries, the CORONA-Mural stereo proposal and its halt, camera configurations including Itek's M-2 and CORONA-J, the 1962 flight summary, and NRO/CIA/Air Force management disputes and funding agreements.

nodes.title: Thorad-Agena launching Vehicle
nodes.summary: A declassified history of the CORONA reconnaissance satellite program, covering the CORONA-J (KH-4A) launches of 1963-1972: early failures, the 1965 Venezuela capsule impact and souvenir-hunting incident, and mission-failure statistics. It details the Thorad-Agena booster and camera upgrades, the 1965 NRO/CIA reorganization and management directive, the J-3 improvement program, the J-3 crop-yield and color film tests, and the 1967-1970 CORONA-HEXAGON overlap debates, cost comparisons, and the final decision to end CORONA procurement. A flight summary table for 1963-1972 is included.

Overview of the CORONA reconnaissance satellite program: its 1960 origins under Eisenhower and Land, rising costs and improved resolution, and Discoverer launch failures and recoveries. Covers 1960-1962 flights, the CORONA-Mural stereo proposal and its halt, cameras (Itek M-2, CORONA-J), and NRO/CIA/Air Force management disputes and funding. Also covers CORONA-J (KH-4A) launches 1963-1972, failures, the 1965 Venezuela capsule incident, Thorad-Agena booster and camera upgrades, the 1965 NRO/CIA reorganization, J-3 improvements and crop-yield/color tests, CORONA-HEXAGON debates, costs, and the end of procurement, with a 1963-1972 flight table.

summary: Section 3 covers CORONA reconnaissance satellite history: Discoverer-XIV's 1960 success (35-foot resolution) and Discoverer-XVIII's improvement (25-foot), Soviet and UN acceptance, security and secrecy measures, and the 1961 creation of the NRO. It also covers the 1962 NRO organization and program rivalries (Samos, E-5/E-6, GAMBIT), CORONA camera developments (C-prime/KH-2, Mural/KH-4), and CORONA's 1960-1972 evolution, failures, management disputes, upgrades, and end of procurement.

title: Section 5
summary: CORONA, begun in 1958, became the first successful space reconnaissance program when a capsule recovered in 1960 returned photographs with 35-40 ft resolution, later improving to 6-10 ft. Capsules grew from 10-16 lb to 80 lb of film, and missions lasted up to 19 days with broad, largely cloud-free coverage. The program flew 145 launches, cost $850 million versus the $59 million estimate, and provided intelligence on Soviet ICBMs and Middle East events. It also paved the way for GAMBIT and HEXAGON.

title: Appendix A

nodes.title: ARC, COMOR and COMIREX
nodes.summary: Covers the history of US imagery-intelligence management: the 1955 ARC for U-2 requirements (chaired by James Reber), the 1959 SIRC for CORONA, the 1960 COMOR merger, and the 1965 NTP and COMIREX creation (with SORS for SIGINT). It describes NPIC under Arthur Lundahl, COMOR's management of CORONA tasking via the NRO and its SOC, CORONA's limited tape-based targeting that later became more flexible, coverage frequency categories, and COMIREX's ten-level priority system with mission simulation.

nodes.title: Overhead Reconnaissance Product Security
nodes.summary: Describes the CIA's early overhead reconnaissance product security: the TALENT system protected aircraft and collections, and TALENT-KEYHOLE (TK) later absorbed spacecraft collections, requiring special clearance and need-to-know. Photo-interpreters received a KH-4 System Manual on CORONA and per-mission operational data such as vehicle attitude, altitude, and solar elevation. Most community members were briefed at the TK level rather than BYEMAN, so CORONA, a BYEMAN program, was known as KH-4.

nodes.title: CORONA Intelligence Achievements
nodes.summary: Describes CORONA, the first US overhead reconnaissance system, which photographed vast denied Soviet areas after the U-2 program ended in 1960. Its achievements include imaging Soviet ICBM, missile test (Plesetsk), submarine (Severodvinsk), and fleet sites; discovering Soviet ABM activity (GALOSH, GRIFFON, SA-5, radars); locating SA-1/2/3/5 defenses for SAC planning; cueing the later GAMBIT system; and providing near-sole source of DMA military mapping data.

summary: Appendix A covers US imagery-intelligence history: the 1955 ARC for U-2 requirements, the 1959 SIRC for CORONA, the 1960 COMOR merger, and the 1965 NTP and COMIREX (with SORS for SIGINT), including NPIC under Lundahl, COMOR's CORONA tasking via NRO, and COMIREX's ten-level priorities. It also covers overhead product security (TALENT, TALENT-KEYHOLE, BYEMAN, KH-4 manuals) and CORONA's achievements: Soviet ICBM, missile, submarine and ABM discoveries, SAM site location, cueing GAMBIT, and DMA mapping data.

title: Appendix B
summary: The text is an appendix (Appendix B, page -138- onward) introducing representative CORONA satellite imagery, described as among the system's most significant contributions to national intelligence production. It consists almost entirely of declassification headers, classification markings (NOFORN-ORCON, BYEMAN/KEYHOLE control), and page-number fragments, with no substantive descriptive content about specific images beyond their illustrative purpose.

title: NOFOIN·OItCON

nodes.title: NOFOIN·OItCON (intro)
nodes.summary: The text is a page from a declassified U.S. government document, approved for release in 2018. It contains only OCR-garbled header and footer markings (NOFORN/ORCON, KEYHOLE control system references), page numbers -156- and -160-, and release stamps. No substantive document content is legible, so the chunk covers no topics beyond classification markings and page numbering.

nodes.title: References
References (intro)
nodes.summary: A declassified CORONA satellite reconnaissance program reference list (roughly items 1-116) with source citations, covering RAND reports, USAF/ARDC/BMD memos and messages, CIA and DoD agreements, ARPA reorientation, NRO organization, interviews, program reviews, and the HEXAGON review, plus a partial glossary of terms (e.g., acetate-base film, ARC, ARPA, AFBMD, Agena, Anti-Ballistic Missile) and handling/classification markings.

nodes.title: CORONA INDEX
nodes.summary: This is a declassified index (Corona index, marked BYEMAN-TALENT-KEYHOLE, approved for release 2018/09/11) listing alphabetized subjects with page references. Entries cover people (e.g., Bissell, Dulles, Johnson, McNamara, Killian), government agencies and offices (CIA, NRO, DoD, DMA, NASA, NSC, USAF), military and satellite programs (Corona, Gambit, Hexagon, Discoverer, Samos, Midas, Mercury, Vanguard), camera systems (C, J, KH series), aircraft and missiles (U-2, SR-71, Thor, Titan, SA-2, SS-9), locations (Venezuela, Soviet Union sites, Vandenberg AFB, Cape Canaveral), and terms like BYEMAN security system and Corona film. Page numbers, photos, illustrations, footnotes, and appendices are cited throughout.

Declassified CORONA satellite reconnaissance reference list (about items 1-116) citing RAND reports, USAF/ARDC/BMD memos, CIA and DoD agreements, ARPA reorientation, NRO organization, interviews, program reviews, and the HEXAGON review, plus a partial glossary and classification markings. Also a declassified alphabetized index (BYEMAN-TALENT-KEYHOLE) covering people, agencies, programs, camera systems, aircraft, missiles, locations, and terms, with page, photo, footnote, and appendix references.

summary: A declassified U.S. government document page (approved for release 2018) with only OCR-garbled NOFORN/ORCON and KEYHOLE markings and page numbers. Its references cover the declassified CORONA satellite reconnaissance program: a list of about 116 items citing RAND reports, USAF/ARDC/BMD memos, CIA and DoD agreements, ARPA reorientation, NRO organization, interviews, program reviews, and the HEXAGON review, plus a partial glossary. It also includes an alphabetized BYEMAN-TALENT-KEYHOLE index of people, agencies, programs, camera systems, aircraft, missiles, locations, and terms.
